Why the others are wrong: **B** the non-assuming buyer risks losing the land but is not personally liable for a deficiency; **A** deficiency judgments are available against personally liable parties; **D** without assumption, the buyer bears no personal liability.

questions.stem: A seller delivers a deed conveying land to a buyer and covenants 'that the grantor is lawfully seized of the estate and has the right to convey it.' Shortly after closing, the buyer discovers the seller did not actually own the land at the moment of conveyance. Which present covenant of title has been breached?

options.text: The covenant of warranty
The covenant of quiet enjoyment
The covenant of seisin
The covenant for further assurances

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The covenant of seisin is a present covenant assuring that the grantor owns the estate purportedly conveyed; it is breached, if at all, at the moment of conveyance when the grantor lacks title. Why the others are wrong: **B** quiet enjoyment is a future covenant breached only upon later eviction by paramount title; **A** the covenant of warranty is also a future covenant requiring disturbance of possession; **D** further assurances obligates the grantor to perfect title later, not a guarantee of present ownership.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller sign a contract for the sale of land. The contract is silent about the quality of title the seller must convey. What quality of title does the law imply the seller must deliver at closing?

options.text: Perfect title with absolutely no defects of any kind
Marketable title, free from reasonable doubt and undue risk of litigation
Whatever title the seller happens to hold, regardless of defects
Title insured by a national title company

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Absent contrary language, every land-sale contract implies a promise to convey marketable title—title reasonably free from doubt that a prudent buyer would accept, without undue risk of litigation. Why the others are wrong: **A** the standard is marketability, not literal perfection; minor, curable defects do not breach it; **C** the seller cannot foist defective title on the buyer; **D** the implied duty is marketable title, not a title insurance policy.

questions.stem: An easement may be created without an express written grant in certain circumstances. Which two of the following can create an easement by implication or operation of law? (Select two.)

options.text: A prior existing use that was apparent, continuous, and reasonably necessary at the time a single parcel is severed
An oral statement that the parties did not intend to bind anyone
Strict necessity arising when a conveyance leaves a parcel landlocked
A neighbor's mere hope of using a path in the future

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** An easement implied from a prior existing use arises when, on severance of commonly owned land, a use was apparent, continuous, and reasonably necessary; an easement by necessity arises when severance leaves a parcel landlocked. Why the others are wrong: **B** a statement disclaiming any intent to bind creates no enforceable easement; **D** a unilateral hope of future use is not a recognized basis for an implied easement.

questions.stem: A homeowner shoots and seriously wounds a teenager who was merely trespassing across the backyard to retrieve a ball, posing no threat of harm to anyone. The teenager sues for battery, and the homeowner claims defense of property. How should a court treat the defense?

options.text: Reject it, because deadly force may not be used merely to defend property
Accept it, because a landowner may always use any force against trespassers
Accept it, because trespassers assume all risks of injury
Reject it only if the teenager was a child of tender years

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A possessor may use only reasonable, non-deadly force to defend property; deadly force is not privileged solely to protect property when no threat to personal safety exists. Why the others are wrong: **B** force in defense of property must be reasonable, never unlimited; **C** trespassers do not forfeit protection against excessive force; **D** the bar on deadly force to protect mere property does not depend on the trespasser's age.

questions.stem: A negligent driver crashes into a utility pole, and a bystander on the sidewalk a block away, who feared for no one in particular and was never in any zone of danger, sues for negligent infliction of emotional distress after merely hearing the crash. Under the majority approach, what is the strongest reason the bystander cannot recover?

options.text: The bystander was outside the zone of danger and was not a close relative who contemporaneously perceived injury to a loved one
Emotional distress damages are never recoverable in negligence
The driver owed a duty to every person who heard the crash
The bystander suffered physical impact, barring recovery

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Most jurisdictions limit bystander NIED to plaintiffs within the zone of danger or, under the Dillon/Thing approach, close relatives who contemporaneously perceive injury to a loved one; a distant, unrelated bystander meets neither test. Why the others are wrong: **B** NIED is recoverable when its requirements are met; **C** duty does not extend to all who merely hear an accident; **D** the facts show no physical impact, and impact would help, not bar, recovery.

questions.stem: A guest slips on a patch of clear liquid in a grocery store. She cannot show how long the liquid was on the floor or that any employee knew of it, but she argues the store should have discovered and cleaned it. To hold the store liable as a land possessor, what must this invitee generally establish about the dangerous condition?

options.text: That the store intended to injure her
That the store had actual or constructive notice of the condition and failed to use reasonable care to remedy or warn
That the store is strictly liable for any injury on the premises
That she was a trespasser owed only a duty to avoid willful harm

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A land possessor owes an invitee a duty of reasonable care, which includes liability for dangerous conditions the possessor knew of or, through reasonable inspection, should have discovered (constructive notice), and failed to fix or warn about. Why the others are wrong: **A** intent is not required for premises negligence; **C** store owners are not strict insurers of customer safety; **D** a paying customer is an invitee, owed the highest duty, not the limited trespasser duty.

questions.stem: A defendant negligently injures a plaintiff who is rushed to a hospital, where a treating physician negligently worsens the injury during care. The plaintiff sues the original defendant for the aggravated harm. Under majority tort principles, is the original defendant liable for the additional harm caused by the physician's negligence?

options.text: Yes, because negligent medical treatment of the injury is a foreseeable intervening cause that does not break the chain of proximate cause
No, because any negligence by a third party is always a superseding cause
No, because the original defendant's duty ended at the hospital door
Yes, but only if the physician's conduct was intentional

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Ordinary negligence by a treating physician in caring for the very injury the defendant caused is a foreseeable intervening cause; it does not sever proximate causation, so the original tortfeasor remains liable for the aggravated harm. Why the others are wrong: **B** foreseeable intervening negligence is not superseding; **C** the defendant's responsibility extends to foreseeable consequences, including negligent treatment; **D** foreseeable negligent (not just intentional) care keeps the original defendant liable.

questions.stem: A plaintiff seeks to invoke res ipsa loquitur to establish a breach of duty without direct evidence of the defendant's specific negligent act. Which two foundational showings does the doctrine traditionally require? (Select two.)

options.text: The defendant intended the harmful result
The harm is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur absent negligence
The plaintiff signed a release before the injury
The instrumentality causing the harm was within the defendant's exclusive control

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** Res ipsa loquitur traditionally requires that the accident be of a type that ordinarily does not happen without negligence and that the instrumentality was within the defendant's exclusive control (and not due to the plaintiff). Why the others are wrong: **A** res ipsa concerns inferring negligence, not intent; intent is irrelevant; **C** a release is a defense to liability, not a foundational element of res ipsa.

questions.stem: A corporation is incorporated in Delaware, and its officers direct, control, and coordinate the company's activities from a single headquarters in Illinois, though most of its factories are in Ohio. For diversity purposes, of which state(s) is the corporation a citizen?

options.text: Delaware and Illinois
Ohio only, where most of its physical operations occur
Every state in which it does any business
Delaware only, because incorporation is the sole test

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1), a corporation is a citizen of both its state of incorporation and the state of its principal place of business, which Hertz v. Friend defines as the 'nerve center' where officers direct and control activities. Why the others are wrong: **B** the nerve center, not the bulk of physical operations, fixes the principal place of business; **C** a corporation is not a citizen of every state where it transacts business; **D** the state of incorporation is only one of the two citizenships.

questions.stem: A plaintiff sues in the Southern District of New York, but the events giving rise to the claim occurred entirely in Texas and the only defendant resides in Texas. The defendant timely moves to transfer to the Northern District of Texas, where the case could have been brought. The forum is otherwise proper. On what basis may the court grant the motion?

options.text: It must dismiss outright, because venue is improper
It may transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) for the convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice
It may transfer only if the New York court lacks personal jurisdiction
It may never transfer a case once it is properly filed

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Section 1404(a) permits a district court, even when venue is proper, to transfer a case to any district where it could have been brought for the convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice. Why the others are wrong: **A** dismissal is the remedy for improper venue under § 1406, but here venue is proper; **C** § 1404(a) transfer does not require a jurisdictional defect; **D** transfer between proper forums is expressly authorized.

questions.stem: A federal trial court enters judgment for the defendant. Twelve days later the plaintiff serves a motion arguing the verdict was against the clear weight of the evidence and asking the court to set the judgment aside and order a new trial. The defendant argues the motion is untimely. Under the Federal Rules, is the motion timely?

options.text: No, because a motion for a new trial must be filed within 10 days
No, because such relief is available only by appeal
Yes, because a Rule 59 motion for a new trial may be filed within 28 days after entry of judgment
Yes, because there is no time limit on new-trial motions

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Under Rule 59(b), a motion for a new trial must be filed no later than 28 days after the entry of judgment, so a motion served on day 12 is timely. Why the others are wrong: **A** the deadline is 28 days, not 10; **B** a new trial is precisely the relief Rule 59 provides in the trial court, separate from appeal; **D** the rule imposes a firm 28-day limit, so the timing is not open-ended.

questions.stem: A defendant who is sued for breach of a supply contract has its own claim against the plaintiff arising from the very same transaction. The defendant wants to assert that claim but worries about waiving it. How does Rule 13 treat this claim?

options.text: It is a compulsory counterclaim that generally must be pleaded in this action or be lost
It is a permissive counterclaim the defendant may freely save for a separate suit
It is a cross-claim that must be asserted against a co-party
It may be raised only by filing a wholly separate lawsuit

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under Rule 13(a), a counterclaim that arises from the same transaction or occurrence as the opposing party's claim is compulsory and must be asserted in the pending action or be forfeited. Why the others are wrong: **B** a permissive counterclaim under 13(b) arises from an unrelated transaction, unlike this same-transaction claim; **C** a cross-claim is asserted against a co-party, not the opposing plaintiff; **D** the claim may and indeed must be raised in the current suit, not deferred to a separate action.

questions.stem: After a defendant answers a complaint without raising any jurisdictional objection, the plaintiff serves discovery seeking documents that are relevant to a claim and proportional to the needs of the case, but the defendant refuses, calling them merely 'background.' The plaintiff moves to compel. Under the current discovery standard, what is the scope of permissible discovery?

options.text: Only evidence that would itself be admissible at trial
Any matter relevant to a party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case
Only documents the requesting party already knows exist
Anything at all, without any limitation

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under Rule 26(b)(1), parties may obtain discovery of any nonprivileged matter relevant to any party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case; information need not be admissible to be discoverable. Why the others are wrong: **A** discovery is broader than admissibility, so the admissibility limit is wrong; **C** a party may seek relevant documents it does not yet know exist; **D** discovery is bounded by relevance, proportionality, and privilege, so it is not limitless.

questions.stem: A plaintiff moves to certify a class under Rule 23. Which two showings must be made in every class action under Rule 23(a)? (Select two.)

options.text: The class is so numerous that joinder of all members is impracticable
The representative parties will fairly and adequately protect the interests of the class
Common questions of law or fact predominate over individual questions
A class action is superior to other available methods of adjudication

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Rule 23(a) requires numerosity, commonality, typicality, and adequacy of representation in every class action; numerosity and adequate representation are among these four prerequisites. Why the others are wrong: **C** predominance is required only for a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class, not every class; **D** superiority is likewise a 23(b)(3) requirement, not a universal Rule 23(a) prerequisite.

questions.stem: Congress, exercising its spending power, offers states federal highway funds on the condition that they raise their drinking age to 21. The condition is clearly stated, relates to highway safety, and the funds at stake are a small fraction of the state's budget. A state challenges the condition. Is the conditional grant a valid exercise of the spending power?

options.text: No, because Congress cannot regulate drinking ages directly, so it cannot do so through spending
Yes, because the condition is unambiguous, related to the federal interest in safe highways, and not unduly coercive
No, because any condition on federal funds violates the Tenth Amendment
Yes, because Congress has unlimited power to attach any condition to spending

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under South Dakota v. Dole, conditions on federal spending are valid if they are clearly stated, relate to a federal interest, do not require unconstitutional action, and are not so coercive as to compel acceptance; a modest, safety-related highway condition satisfies this. Why the others are wrong: **A** Congress may use the spending power to induce conduct it could not command directly; **C** properly framed conditions on funds do not violate the Tenth Amendment; **D** the spending power is bounded by the Dole limits, so it is not unlimited.

questions.stem: A state enacts a law that requires a 30-day waiting period and a showing of good cause before any resident may obtain a permit to travel to and settle in another state. A resident challenges it. Which constitutional principle most directly invalidates the restriction?

options.text: The fundamental right to interstate travel, burdened by the restriction, triggers heightened scrutiny the law cannot survive
The Second Amendment right to bear arms
The Contracts Clause
The Eleventh Amendment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The right to interstate travel is a fundamental right; a state law that directly penalizes or conditions the ability to move to and settle in another state is reviewed under strict scrutiny and will almost always fail. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Second Amendment concerns firearms, not travel; **C** the Contracts Clause limits impairment of existing contracts, not movement; **D** the Eleventh Amendment concerns suits against states, not the right to travel.

questions.stem: The President directs the seizure of private steel mills to keep them operating during a labor dispute, citing no specific statute and acting contrary to the procedure Congress had established for such disputes. A mill owner challenges the seizure. Under separation-of-powers analysis, why is the President's action most likely invalid?

options.text: Because the President was acting against the implied will of Congress, where presidential power is at its lowest ebb and no independent constitutional authority supports the seizure
Because the President may never act without an express constitutional clause
Because the Commerce Clause forbids any federal control of industry
Because the Tenth Amendment reserves all industrial regulation to the states

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the Youngstown framework, when the President acts contrary to the expressed or implied will of Congress, his power is at its lowest ebb and can be sustained only by his own constitutional authority minus Congress's; absent such authority, the domestic seizure is invalid. Why the others are wrong: **B** the President has inherent executive powers and need not point to an express clause for every act; **C** the Commerce Clause does not bar all federal involvement in industry; **D** the Tenth Amendment does not strip the federal government of all industrial authority.

questions.stem: A state imposes a generally applicable, neutral criminal law banning the use of a particular controlled substance. A religious group used the substance in sincere worship rituals and challenges the law as applied to them under the Free Exercise Clause. Under the prevailing federal constitutional standard, how is the neutral law of general applicability reviewed?

options.text: It is subject to strict scrutiny because it incidentally burdens religious practice
It is valid as long as it is neutral and generally applicable, even if it incidentally burdens religious conduct
It is automatically invalid whenever it conflicts with any religious practice
It is reviewed only under the Establishment Clause

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under Employment Division v. Smith, a neutral law of general applicability that only incidentally burdens religious conduct does not violate the Free Exercise Clause and is not subject to strict scrutiny. Why the others are wrong: **A** strict scrutiny applies to laws that target religion or are not generally applicable, not neutral general laws; **C** a neutral general law is not automatically void merely because it conflicts with a religious practice; **D** the challenge sounds in free exercise, not the Establishment Clause.

questions.stem: A state law sets the age of eligibility for certain commercial driving permits at 21 for men but 18 for women, citing accident statistics. A 19-year-old man challenges the distinction under the Equal Protection Clause. What standard of review applies and what must the state show?

options.text: Rational basis: the state need only show the line is rationally related to a legitimate interest
Strict scrutiny: the classification must be narrowly tailored to a compelling interest
Intermediate scrutiny: the gender classification must be substantially related to an important government interest
No review, because driving is a privilege rather than a right

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Classifications based on gender are quasi-suspect and reviewed under intermediate scrutiny, requiring the state to show the line is substantially related to an important governmental interest and rests on an exceedingly persuasive justification. Why the others are wrong: **A** rational basis is too deferential for a sex-based classification; **B** strict scrutiny applies to race, national origin, and alienage, not gender; **D** that driving is a privilege does not exempt a gender classification from equal protection review.

questions.stem: A litigant in federal court asks the court to decide a question. Which two situations would most likely lead a federal court to decline on justiciability grounds? (Select two.)

options.text: The plaintiff seeks an advisory opinion on a hypothetical statute that has not been enacted or applied to anyone
The plaintiff has suffered a concrete injury traceable to the defendant and redressable by the court
The question is one the Constitution textually commits to another branch and lacks judicially manageable standards
The case presents a live, ongoing dispute between adverse parties

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Federal courts will not issue advisory opinions on hypothetical or unapplied laws, and they will decline nonjusticiable political questions textually committed to another branch and lacking manageable standards. Why the others are wrong: **B** a concrete, traceable, redressable injury satisfies standing, so the court would hear it; **D** a live dispute between adverse parties is exactly what makes a case justiciable.

questions.stem: A homeowner mails a written offer to a contractor to repair a roof, and the contractor mails back a properly addressed and stamped acceptance. Before that acceptance arrives, the homeowner phones the contractor to revoke. The contractor had already deposited the acceptance in the mail. Under the common law, when was the contract formed?

options.text: When the acceptance was dispatched into the mail, under the mailbox rule
When the homeowner received the acceptance
Never, because the revocation was effective first
When the homeowner originally mailed the offer

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the mailbox rule, an acceptance is effective upon dispatch, so a contract formed the moment the contractor deposited the properly addressed acceptance, and the later revocation came too late. Why the others are wrong: **B** receipt governs revocations and rejections, not acceptances under the mailbox rule; **C** the revocation was effective only on receipt, after acceptance had already been dispatched; **D** mailing an offer does not by itself form a contract without acceptance.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old buys a non-necessity electronic gadget on credit, using it for two months. Shortly after turning 18, and without doing anything to ratify the deal, she returns the gadget and demands her payments back, disaffirming the contract. The seller refuses, citing the signed agreement. What is the legal effect of the buyer's status when she contracted?

options.text: The contract was void from the start and never existed
The contract was fully enforceable because she received the goods
The contract was voidable at the minor's option, and she may disaffirm a non-necessity contract
The contract is enforceable because electronics are necessities

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A contract by a minor for non-necessities is voidable at the minor's election; she may disaffirm during minority or within a reasonable time after reaching majority, provided she has not ratified. Why the others are wrong: **A** the contract is voidable, not void—it has legal effect until disaffirmed; **B** receiving the goods does not strip the minor of the power to disaffirm a non-necessity; **D** an ordinary electronic gadget is not a necessity such as food, shelter, or medical care.

questions.stem: A contractor agrees to build a house and is to be paid only after an architect issues a written certificate that the work conforms to the plans. The contractor completes the work properly, but the architect arbitrarily and in bad faith refuses to issue the certificate. The owner refuses to pay, pointing to the missing certificate. What is the contractor's best argument?

options.text: The express condition of architect certification is excused because its non-occurrence was caused by the bad-faith refusal, and substantial performance entitles him to payment
The condition must be strictly enforced, so the contractor cannot recover
The contractor may recover only in tort, not contract
The owner's duty to pay was never triggered and cannot be excused

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A party cannot rely on the non-occurrence of a condition that it (or its agent) wrongfully prevented; the architect's bad-faith refusal excuses the certification condition, and the contractor's substantial performance triggers the duty to pay. Why the others are wrong: **B** wrongful prevention excuses strict enforcement of the condition; **C** the contractor's remedy lies in contract for the price, not only in tort; **D** the condition is excused, so the duty to pay is triggered.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller have a written contract for the sale of goods to be delivered in six months. Three months before delivery, the seller sends the buyer an unequivocal written statement that it will not deliver under any circumstances. The buyer wants to sue at once rather than wait for the delivery date. May the buyer treat this as a present breach?

options.text: No, because no breach can occur before the performance date arrives
Yes, because a clear, unequivocal repudiation before performance is an anticipatory repudiation that lets the non-breaching party sue immediately
No, because the buyer must first demand assurances and wait 60 days
Yes, but only if the buyer has already paid in full

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An unequivocal repudiation before the time for performance is an anticipatory repudiation, permitting the aggrieved party to treat the contract as breached and sue immediately or await performance. Why the others are wrong: **A** anticipatory repudiation is precisely an exception allowing suit before the performance date; **C** demanding assurances is an option where there are mere reasonable grounds for insecurity, not where there is a clear repudiation; **D** the right to sue on a repudiation does not depend on prepayment.

questions.stem: A debtor owes a creditor $5,000 on an undisputed, past-due debt. The creditor agrees to accept $3,000 in full satisfaction, and the debtor pays the $3,000. The creditor then sues for the remaining $2,000. Under the common-law pre-existing duty rule, may the creditor recover the balance?

options.text: Yes, because the debtor gave no new consideration for the creditor's promise to discharge the undisputed debt
No, because partial payment of an undisputed debt always discharges the whole
No, because any agreement to take less is automatically binding
Yes, but only if the original debt was oral

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Paying part of an amount one is already legally obligated to pay on an undisputed, liquidated debt is not consideration for a promise to forgive the rest; absent new consideration or an accord device, the creditor may still recover the $2,000 balance. Why the others are wrong: **B** part payment of a liquidated, undisputed debt does not by itself discharge the whole; **C** a bare promise to accept less, without consideration, is not binding; **D** the result does not turn on whether the debt was oral.

questions.stem: A party seeks to rescind a contract on the ground of a mutual mistake of fact. Which two requirements must generally be met for rescission on that basis? (Select two.)

options.text: The mistake concerned a basic assumption on which the contract was made
The mistake related merely to one party's prediction of future market value
The mistake had a material effect on the agreed exchange of performances
The party seeking relief bore the risk of the mistake under the agreement

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Rescission for mutual mistake requires that the mistake concern a basic assumption underlying the contract and have a material effect on the agreed exchange, with the adversely affected party not bearing the risk. Why the others are wrong: **B** an erroneous prediction about future market value is not a mistake of existing fact and is not a ground for rescission; **D** if the party seeking relief bore the risk of the mistake, rescission is barred, so that defeats rather than supports relief.

questions.stem: A defendant, provoked into a sudden heat of passion by a serious and legally adequate provocation, kills the provoker immediately and before any reasonable opportunity to cool off. He had no prior intent to kill. At common law, of what homicide is he most likely guilty?

options.text: First-degree murder
Voluntary manslaughter
Involuntary manslaughter
No crime, because adequate provocation is a complete defense

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A killing committed in a sudden heat of passion arising from legally adequate provocation, before a reasonable cooling-off period, is voluntary manslaughter; the provocation mitigates murder rather than excusing the killing. Why the others are wrong: **A** adequate provocation negates the malice required for murder, so it is not first-degree murder; **C** involuntary manslaughter involves criminal negligence or an unlawful act, not an intentional heat-of-passion killing; **D** provocation is only a partial defense that mitigates, not a complete defense.

questions.stem: A defendant points an unloaded gun at a store clerk, threatens her, and demands cash; the frightened clerk hands over money from the register. The defendant is charged with robbery. He argues it cannot be robbery because the gun was unloaded. Has a robbery occurred?

options.text: Yes, because robbery is a taking of property from a person by force or intimidation, and the threat with the gun supplied the intimidation
No, because an unloaded gun cannot create a real threat
No, because the clerk voluntarily handed over the money
No, because robbery requires actual physical contact with the victim

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Robbery is larceny from the person or presence of the victim accomplished by force or by putting the victim in fear; a threatening demand at gunpoint supplies the intimidation even if the gun is unloaded. Why the others are wrong: **B** the victim's reasonable fear, not the gun's actual capacity, is what matters; **C** property handed over out of fear is taken by intimidation, not given voluntarily; **D** robbery requires force or fear, not necessarily physical contact.

questions.stem: Two people agree to rob a store and begin driving toward it with weapons. Before reaching the store, one of them has a change of heart, tells the other he is out, and drives away, leaving the plan. He is later charged with conspiracy. Under the majority common-law approach, does his change of heart undo the conspiracy?

options.text: No, because the conspiracy was complete upon the agreement, and withdrawal does not erase liability for the conspiracy itself
Yes, because abandonment is always a complete defense to conspiracy
Yes, because withdrawal automatically dissolves the agreement for all conspirators
No, but only because he kept the weapons

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Common-law conspiracy is complete once the unlawful agreement is formed (plus an overt act where required); a later withdrawal may limit liability for subsequent crimes of co-conspirators but does not undo liability for the conspiracy already formed. Why the others are wrong: **B** withdrawal is not a complete defense to the conspiracy charge itself at common law; **C** one conspirator's withdrawal does not dissolve the agreement as to the others; **D** liability for the conspiracy attaches regardless of what he did with the weapons.

questions.stem: A suspect in custody is given Miranda warnings, then clearly and unambiguously states, 'I want a lawyer before I say anything.' Officers nonetheless continue questioning him about the same crime without counsel present, and he confesses. Under the Fifth Amendment, what is the effect of continuing the interrogation?

options.text: The confession is admissible because the warnings were given
The confession must be suppressed, because once a suspect clearly invokes the right to counsel, interrogation must cease until counsel is present or the suspect reinitiates
The confession is admissible because the suspect spoke voluntarily
The confession is admissible if officers waited five minutes before resuming

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under Edwards v. Arizona, once a suspect unambiguously invokes the Miranda right to counsel, all interrogation must stop until counsel is present unless the suspect himself reinitiates communication; a confession obtained by continued questioning is inadmissible. Why the others are wrong: **A** giving warnings does not permit ignoring a clear invocation; **C** continued interrogation after invocation taints the statement regardless of apparent voluntariness; **D** a brief pause does not cure the Edwards violation.

questions.stem: Two private parties argue, and one suddenly punches the other in the face, causing a bruise but no lasting harm; the puncher intended the blow. He is charged with a crime for the unconsented harmful contact. Which offense most precisely describes the completed harmful touching?

options.text: Battery
Attempt
Solicitation
Kidnapping

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Criminal battery is the unlawful application of force to another resulting in bodily harm or an offensive touching; an intentional punch causing a bruise is a completed battery. Why the others are wrong: **B** attempt applies when the crime is not completed, but here the harmful contact occurred; **C** solicitation involves enticing another to commit a crime, which did not happen; **D** kidnapping requires unlawful confinement and movement of a person, not present here.

questions.stem: A defendant raises self-defense to a charge that he used force against another. Under general common-law principles, which two requirements must be satisfied for a non-aggressor's use of ordinary (non-deadly) force in self-defense to be justified? (Select two.)

options.text: The defendant reasonably believed force was necessary to protect against an imminent unlawful threat
The defendant used force grossly disproportionate to the threat
The force used was proportional to the threat faced
The defendant was the initial aggressor who provoked the encounter

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Self-defense by a non-aggressor requires a reasonable belief that force is necessary to repel an imminent unlawful threat and the use of force proportional to that threat. Why the others are wrong: **B** grossly disproportionate force exceeds the privilege and is not justified; **D** being the initial aggressor generally forfeits the right to claim self-defense absent withdrawal, so it undermines rather than supports the defense.

questions.stem: At a witness's deposition before trial, the witness testified one way; at trial she testifies differently. To impeach her, the cross-examiner offers her prior inconsistent deposition statement. The deposition was given under oath. For what purpose is this prior inconsistent statement admissible under the Federal Rules?

options.text: For impeachment, and also substantively, because a prior inconsistent statement made under oath at a deposition is not hearsay under FRE 801(d)(1)(A)
For no purpose, because prior statements are always inadmissible hearsay
Only to prove the witness's bias
Only after the witness is declared unavailable

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under FRE 801(d)(1)(A), a declarant-witness's prior inconsistent statement is not hearsay and is admissible substantively if it was given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, or other proceeding such as a deposition; it also impeaches. Why the others are wrong: **B** the rule specifically removes such sworn prior inconsistent statements from hearsay; **C** the statement does more than show bias—it can be used for its truth; **D** the witness must be testifying and subject to cross, not unavailable.

questions.stem: In a wrongful-death suit, a plaintiff offers a hospital's routine business record—a chart entry made by a nurse at the time of treatment, in the regular course of the hospital's activity, as a regular practice. The defense objects that it is hearsay. Under the Federal Rules, on what basis is the chart most likely admissible?

options.text: As a present sense impression only
As a record of a regularly conducted activity (business record) under FRE 803(6)
It is inadmissible because all hospital records are hearsay
Only if the nurse is unavailable to testify

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under FRE 803(6), a record kept in the regular course of a regularly conducted activity, made at or near the time by someone with knowledge as a regular practice, is admissible if those conditions are shown and there is no indication of untrustworthiness. Why the others are wrong: **A** the present sense impression is a different exception with stricter contemporaneity requirements; **C** business records are an established hearsay exception, so they are not categorically barred; **D** Rule 803 exceptions apply regardless of the declarant's availability.

questions.stem: After a car accident, the defendant driver had no insurance, and the plaintiff offers evidence that the defendant was uninsured to suggest he was a careless person who caused the crash. The defendant objects. How should the court rule on admitting the lack of insurance to prove negligence?

options.text: Admit it, because financial status is always relevant
Exclude it, because evidence that a person was or was not insured against liability is not admissible to prove whether the person acted negligently or wrongfully
Admit it, because it shows the defendant's motive to drive carefully
Exclude it as a violation of the best evidence rule

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under FRE 411, evidence that a person was or was not insured against liability is inadmissible to prove whether the person acted negligently or otherwise wrongfully, though it may be admissible for other purposes such as proving agency or bias. Why the others are wrong: **A** insurance status is not freely admissible to show carelessness; **C** lack of insurance is not offered here for a permitted purpose like bias or ownership, but to prove negligence, which Rule 411 forbids; **D** the best evidence rule concerns proving the contents of writings, not insurance status.

questions.stem: In a battery prosecution where the defendant claims self-defense, the defendant seeks to offer evidence of the alleged victim's character for violence to show the victim was the first aggressor. The prosecution objects. Under the Federal Rules, how should the court treat this character evidence about the victim?

options.text: Exclude it, because a defendant may never offer evidence about a victim's character
Admit it, because a criminal defendant may offer evidence of a pertinent trait of the alleged victim, such as a violent character to show the victim was the aggressor
Admit it, but only as specific instances the defendant personally witnessed
Exclude it as improper propensity evidence in all circumstances

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under FRE 404(a)(2), a criminal defendant may offer evidence of a pertinent character trait of the alleged victim—here, the victim's violent character—to support a self-defense claim that the victim was the first aggressor, subject to the prosecution's rebuttal. Why the others are wrong: **A** the rules specifically allow a defendant to offer pertinent victim-character evidence; **C** in the criminal case-in-chief such character is proved by reputation or opinion, not limited to instances the defendant saw; **D** this is a recognized exception to the propensity ban, so it is not always excluded.

questions.stem: A patient sues her doctor and, to prove a contested fact, seeks to compel disclosure of confidential communications she made to the doctor for the purpose of diagnosis and treatment. The patient herself put her medical condition directly at issue by filing the claim. May the doctor invoke the physician-patient privilege to block the disclosure?

options.text: No, because the patient waived the privilege by placing her physical condition at issue in the litigation
Yes, because the privilege is absolute and can never be waived
Yes, because only the doctor holds the privilege
No, because there is no recognized physician-patient privilege at all

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The physician-patient privilege belongs to the patient and is waived when the patient affirmatively places her physical or mental condition at issue, as by suing for that condition. Why the others are wrong: **B** the privilege is not absolute and is subject to waiver; **C** the privilege is held by the patient, not the doctor, who asserts it on the patient's behalf; **D** the privilege exists by statute in most jurisdictions, so denying its existence is wrong.

questions.stem: A judge must decide whether to exclude relevant evidence under FRE 403. Which two of the following are recognized grounds on which a court may exclude otherwise relevant evidence under that rule? (Select two.)

options.text: The evidence's probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of unfair prejudice
The evidence is merely unfavorable to the objecting party's case
The evidence would needlessly present cumulative evidence and waste time
The evidence was offered by the opposing party rather than the proponent

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** FRE 403 permits exclusion of relevant evidence when its probative value is substantially outweighed by dangers such as unfair prejudice, or by considerations like needlessly presenting cumulative evidence and undue delay or waste of time. Why the others are wrong: **B** evidence is not excludable merely because it is damaging—only unfair prejudice counts; **D** the identity of the offering party is not a Rule 403 ground for exclusion.

questions.stem: A tenant under a valid lease assigns the entire remaining term to a third party, who takes possession. The lease did not prohibit assignment. The assignee fails to pay rent. The landlord, who never released the original tenant, seeks rent. From whom may the landlord recover?

options.text: From the assignee under privity of estate and from the original tenant under privity of contract
From the assignee only, because the original tenant is automatically released by an assignment
From the original tenant only, because the assignee has no obligations
From neither, because assignment terminates the lease

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** After an assignment, the assignee is in privity of estate with the landlord and liable for rent that accrues while in possession, while the original tenant remains liable in privity of contract unless the landlord releases him. Why the others are wrong: **B** an assignment does not by itself release the original tenant; **C** the assignee in privity of estate is liable for rent accruing during the assignment; **D** assignment transfers the leasehold but does not terminate the lease.

questions.stem: A homeowner installs a large built-in bookcase by bolting it to the wall studs and integrating it with the room's trim, intending it to remain permanently. She later sells the home under a contract silent about the bookcase. At closing she tries to remove it, claiming it is her personal property. Who is entitled to the bookcase?

options.text: The buyer, because the bookcase became a fixture that passes with the realty
The seller, because anything she bought remains her personal property forever
The seller, because chattels can never become part of real property
Neither, because the contract's silence voids any transfer of the item

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A chattel that is annexed to land with the intent that it become a permanent part of the realty becomes a fixture and passes with the land unless the contract reserves it; a bolted-in, integrated bookcase qualifies. Why the others are wrong: **B** personal property can lose that character once it becomes a fixture; **C** chattels routinely become real property as fixtures; **D** silence does not void the sale—it means the fixture passes with the land.

questions.stem: In a lien-theory jurisdiction, a homeowner gives a first mortgage to Bank One in January, which records immediately, and then a second mortgage to Bank Two in June, which also records. The homeowner defaults, and Bank One forecloses. As between the two mortgages, what is the effect of the foreclosure on Bank Two's interest?

options.text: Foreclosure by the senior mortgagee generally extinguishes the junior mortgage as a lien on the property, leaving the junior lender to claim any surplus proceeds
Foreclosure by the senior leaves the junior lien fully intact on the land
The junior mortgage automatically becomes senior upon foreclosure
Both mortgages are wiped out, including the foreclosing senior lender's

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Foreclosure by a senior mortgagee terminates junior interests in the property as liens; the junior lender's recourse is to any surplus from the sale and to the debtor personally, not to the foreclosed land. Why the others are wrong: **B** a properly conducted senior foreclosure does not leave the junior lien on the property; **C** priority is fixed by recording order, and foreclosure does not promote a junior lien; **D** the foreclosing senior lender's interest is satisfied first, not wiped out.

questions.stem: Two people own land as tenants in common, each holding an undivided one-half interest. The relationship sours and one cotenant wants to end the co-ownership and obtain his separate share. The other refuses to cooperate in any sale or division. What remedy is available to the cotenant who wants out?

options.text: An action for partition, by physical division or by sale and division of the proceeds
Nothing, because cotenants are bound together for life
Adverse possession against the other cotenant after one year
Automatic forfeiture of the uncooperative cotenant's share

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Any cotenant has the right to seek partition to end a concurrent estate—either partition in kind (physical division) or, where division is impractical, partition by sale with the proceeds divided according to ownership shares. Why the others are wrong: **B** cotenancy is not perpetual; partition is available; **C** mere co-ownership is not hostile, so ordinary possession does not ripen into adverse possession against a cotenant; **D** refusing to cooperate does not forfeit a cotenant's interest.

questions.stem: A neighbor claims a prescriptive easement to use a path across an adjoining owner's land. Which two elements must the claimant generally establish to acquire an easement by prescription? (Select two.)

options.text: Use that was open and notorious
Use that was permissive and with the owner's consent
Use that was continuous for the statutory period
Payment of the property taxes on the servient parcel

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** A prescriptive easement requires use that is open and notorious, adverse (hostile, without permission), and continuous for the statutory period—mirroring adverse possession but yielding a use right rather than title. Why the others are wrong: **B** permissive use defeats the adversity required, so consent prevents prescription; **D** paying taxes on the servient land is not an element of prescriptive easement.

questions.stem: A practical joker, intending to cause severe emotional distress, falsely tells an elderly woman that her son has just been killed in a horrific accident. The woman suffers severe emotional distress as a result, though no physical impact occurred. She sues. Which tort theory best supports recovery?

options.text: Intentional infliction of emotional distress, based on extreme and outrageous conduct intended to cause severe emotional distress
Battery, because words can constitute a harmful contact
Negligence per se
Trespass to chattels

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Intentional infliction of emotional distress requires extreme and outrageous conduct, intent or recklessness, causation, and severe emotional distress; deliberately fabricating news of a loved one's death is the classic example. Why the others are wrong: **B** battery requires a harmful or offensive physical contact, which words alone do not supply; **C** negligence per se involves violating a safety statute, not an intentional cruel hoax; **D** trespass to chattels concerns interference with personal property, not emotional harm.

questions.stem: A pedestrian is struck when a driver, momentarily distracted, runs onto the sidewalk. To prove that the driver's conduct was a cause in fact of her injuries in a straightforward single-cause case, which test does the plaintiff most directly rely on?

options.text: The 'but-for' test: the harm would not have occurred but for the defendant's conduct
Whether the defendant intended the harm
Whether the defendant violated a contract
Whether the plaintiff signed a waiver

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Actual causation in a single-cause case is generally established by the but-for test: the plaintiff's harm would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligent conduct. Why the others are wrong: **B** intent is irrelevant to causation in negligence, which turns on the causal link, not purpose; **C** breach of contract is a separate basis of liability, not the test for tort causation; **D** a waiver is a potential defense, not the measure of actual cause.

questions.stem: A demolition company uses dynamite to blast rock on a job site in a residential area, taking every reasonable precaution. Despite this care, the vibrations crack the foundation of a neighboring home. The homeowner sues. Under the majority approach, on what basis is the company most likely liable?

options.text: Strict liability, because blasting is an abnormally dangerous activity for which liability attaches regardless of due care
Not liable, because it exercised reasonable care
Liable only if it intended to damage the home
Not liable, because the homeowner could have reinforced the foundation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Blasting with explosives is a classic abnormally dangerous activity; one who carries it on is strictly liable for resulting harm even if reasonable care was used, because the activity creates a high risk that cannot be eliminated by care. Why the others are wrong: **B** due care is not a defense to strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities; **C** strict liability does not require intent to harm; **D** the homeowner's failure to fortify against blasting is not a recognized bar to recovery here.

questions.stem: A consumer is injured by a power tool she bought from a hardware retailer. The defect was a flaw in the tool's design that made it unreasonably dangerous, and the retailer sold it in the ordinary course of business without altering it. She sues the retailer in strict products liability. May a non-manufacturing commercial seller in the distribution chain be held strictly liable?

options.text: Yes, because any commercial seller in the distribution chain of a defective product may be held strictly liable
No, because only the manufacturer can ever be strictly liable
No, because the retailer did not create the defect
Yes, but only if the retailer also gave an express warranty

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Strict products liability extends to any commercial seller engaged in the business of selling the product, including retailers and distributors in the chain of distribution, not just the manufacturer. Why the others are wrong: **B** liability is not limited to manufacturers; downstream commercial sellers are included; **C** a seller need not have created the defect to be strictly liable for distributing a defective product; **D** an express warranty is a separate theory and is not required for strict liability.

questions.stem: A plaintiff sues a defendant for the tort of false imprisonment. Which two elements must the plaintiff generally establish? (Select two.)

options.text: The defendant intended to confine the plaintiff within boundaries fixed by the defendant
The plaintiff suffered permanent physical injury
The plaintiff was actually confined and either was aware of the confinement or was harmed by it
The defendant published a defamatory statement about the plaintiff

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** False imprisonment requires an act intended to confine the plaintiff within boundaries fixed by the defendant, resulting in actual confinement, of which the plaintiff is aware or by which the plaintiff is harmed. Why the others are wrong: **B** permanent physical injury is not required; the dignitary harm of confinement suffices; **D** publishing a defamatory statement is an element of defamation, not false imprisonment.
